excerpt: 25 November 2026 In which a traveling salesman digs π out of LLM temperature math by Yours Truly You’ve probably typed temperature: 0.7 into an LLM API payload at some point in the last few years. Or you’ve heard there’s some “temperature” in the AI stack and filed it under “weird stuff people get paid tons of money for”. It isn’t that weird, but don’t take my word for it. Roughly, and going on vibes: turn the temperature down to 0.0 and the model gets unimaginative and sees red tape everywhere. Turn it up to 1.8 and it switches languages mid-sentence and closes brackets it didn’t open yet. So why does this post also have \(\pi\) and a traveling salesman in it? Because that “temperature” has a past. It wandered in from 19th-century statistical mechanics and made itself at home in machine learning. And once you see where the equation comes from, you start seeing ways to abuse it. Today’s abuse: we take the Boltzmann temperature math behind LLM token sampling, hand it to an NP-hard optimization problem on a unit circle, write a small solver for it, and dig the number \(\pi\) out of the rubble. I promise I won’t cheat. (We’ll get to what “cheating” means in a minute.) Contents So what is temperature in an LLM? At the end of a forward pass, a language model hands you a big vector of raw, unnormalized scores, one per token in its vocabulary, and leaves picking the word to you. People call those scores logits, and we’ll write them as \(z_1, z_2, \dots, z_V\). To turn the scores into probabilities we can sample from, we run them through softmax, dividing the logits by a positive number \(T\) on the way in: \[P_i = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j / T}}\] Look at the numerator for a second: \(e^{z_i / T}\). If you took a thermodynamics class in college and have since suppressed the memories, sorry, I’m about to bring one back: the Boltzmann distribution.
